expectedText:
PROPERTY TAX PARENT-CHILD TRANSFER EXCLUSION (PROPOSITION 19) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 · 123-456-789

TRANSFER AND CLAIM DECLARATION
This information sheet describes California's property tax reassessment exclusion for a transfer of real property located at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, Assessor's Parcel Number 123-456-789, between Pat Morgan ("Transferor") and Jordan Lee ("Transferee"), who is Transferor's Child. This exclusion is set out in California Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2, enacted to implement Article XIII A, Section 2.1 of the California Constitution (added by Proposition 19, approved by California voters on November 3, 2020), for transfers occurring on or after February 16, 2021.

This declaration is a factual record of the parties, relationship, and property involved. It is not itself the claim for exclusion that Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(b) requires to be filed with the county assessor on the form the State Board of Equalization prescribes, and completing it does not determine that this transfer in fact qualifies for exclusion from reassessment, does not determine whether the property has become or will become Jordan Lee's principal residence, and does not determine whether the property qualifies as a family farm.

EFFECTIVE DATE AND TRANSITION FROM THE FORMER PARENT-CHILD EXCLUSION
The California property tax reassessment exclusion for transfers between parents and children, and between grandparents and grandchildren, changed substantially as a result of Proposition 19, a constitutional amendment California voters approved on November 3, 2020. Before that measure, Article XIII A, Section 2(h) of the California Constitution excluded from "change in ownership" a principal-residence transfer between parents and children, along with the first $1,000,000 of full cash value of other real property transferred between them, without requiring the transferee to use the property as a principal residence. A new constitutional provision added by Proposition 19, Article XIII A, Section 2.1(d), makes that former provision, Section 2(h), inoperative for any purchase or transfer occurring on or after February 16, 2021, while continuing to apply Section 2(h) to any purchase or transfer that occurred on or before February 15, 2021. Consistent with that constitutional transition, the statute enacted to implement the new rule, Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2, states that its exclusion applies beginning on and after that same date, February 16, 2021. The older implementing statute, Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.1 — which does not itself state a principal-residence-use requirement for the transferee, as described in this document's clause on that requirement — continues, by its own terms, to apply to transfers of real property completed on or after November 6, 1986, but its practical effect for transfers after February 15, 2021 depends on the fact that its constitutional authorization was made inoperative by Section 2.1(d), rather than on any cutoff date written into Section 63.1's own statutory text.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Subdivision (h) of Section 2 shall apply to any purchase or transfer that occurs on or before February 15, 2021, but shall not apply to any purchase or transfer occurring after that date. Subdivision (h) of Section 2 shall be inoperative as of February 16, 2021."
  — Cal. Const. art. XIII A, § 2.1(d), California Constitution, transition provision making the former Section 2(h) exclusion inoperative for transfers on or after February 16, 2021 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.+2.1.&article=XIII+A)
  "Notwithstanding any provision of this chapter, beginning on and after February 16, 2021, a change in ownership shall not include, in whole or in part, any of the following purchases or transfers for which a claim is filed:"
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 63.2(a), California Revenue and Taxation Code, effective date of the current parent-child/grandparent-grandchild exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=63.2.)
  Known gap: This draws on two separately enacted sources treated here as independent: Article XIII A, Section 2.1(d) of the California Constitution (added by the Proposition 19 ballot initiative) and Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a) (implementing legislation, since amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 539 (SB 293)). Correction to a natural assumption: a reader consulting only the current text of Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.1 will not find any statement there that it stopped applying to transfers on or after February 16, 2021 — that limit is not written into Section 63.1 itself. It arises instead because Section 63.1 implements the constitutional exclusion in the former Article XIII A, Section 2(h), and Section 2.1(d) separately makes Section 2(h) inoperative for later transfers. This clause does not itself apply either statute to any specific reader's transfer, and does not determine which statute's exclusion mechanism governs any particular transaction.

REQUIREMENT THAT THE PROPERTY BECOME THE TRANSFEREE'S PRINCIPAL RESIDENCE
Under the current parent-child and grandparent-grandchild exclusion, a transfer of a family home qualifies only if the property was the transferor's principal residence and becomes the transferee's principal residence within one year of the transfer. Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(1)(A)-(C) states that the transferee must also file for the homeowners' exemption or the disabled veterans' exemption within a year of the transfer, and that the exclusion is removed — with the property's base year value re-enrolled as it would otherwise have stood, adjusted for inflation and new construction — as of the lien date immediately following the date the transferee (or a later eligible transferee who timely filed for the exemption) stops being eligible for either exemption. Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(5) of the California Constitution states the same exemption-filing mechanism: the transferee must claim the homeowners' or disabled veterans' exemption at the time of the transfer to receive the benefit immediately, but a transferee who misses that timing may still claim the benefit by filing for the exemption within one year of the transfer, in which case the transferee is entitled to a refund of taxes paid between the transfer date and the date the exemption is claimed. This is a change from the exclusion that applied before February 16, 2021: the former constitutional exclusion, Article XIII A, Section 2(h)(1), excluded a transfer of "the principal residence of the transferor" between parents and children without requiring that the property become the transferee's principal residence at all, and without any homeowners'- or disabled-veterans'-exemption filing condition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The transfer is required to be of a principal residence of the transferor, and become the principal residence of the transferee within one year of the transfer.(B) The transferee shall file for the homeowners’ or disabled veterans’ exemption within a year of the transfer, and the exclusion shall be removed on the date an eligible transferee, or a subsequent eligible transferee who files for the homeowners’ or disabled veterans’ exemption within one year, is no longer eligible for either the homeowners’ or disabled veterans’ exemption.(C) If applicable, as of the lien date immediately following the date the eligible transferee or subsequent eligible transferee no longer qualifies for the exclusion provided by this section, the base year value established as of the change in ownership date to which the exclusion applied, adjusted annually in accordance with paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 51, shall be enrolled."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 63.2(a)(1)(A)-(C), California Revenue and Taxation Code, principal-residence and homeowners'/disabled veterans' exemption-filing requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=63.2.)
  "in order to receive the property tax benefit provided by this section for the purchase or transfer of a family home, the transferee shall claim the homeowner’s exemption or disabled veteran’s exemption at the time of the purchase or transfer of the family home.(B) A transferee who fails to claim the homeowner’s exemption or disabled veteran’s exemption at the time of the purchase or transfer of the family home may receive the property tax benefit provided by this section by claiming the homeowner’s exemption or disabled veteran’s exemption within one year of the purchase or transfer of the family home and shall be entitled to a refund of taxes previously owed or paid between the date of the transfer and the date the transferee claims the homeowner's exemption or disabled veteran’s exemption."
  — Cal. Const. art. XIII A, § 2.1(c)(5), California Constitution, timing for claiming the homeowners' or disabled veterans' exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.+2.1.&article=XIII+A)
  "the terms “purchased” and “change in ownership” do not include the purchase or transfer of the principal residence of the transferor in the case of a purchase or transfer between parents and their children, as defined by the Legislature, and the purchase or transfer of the first one million dollars ($1,000,000) of the full cash value of all other real property between parents and their children, as defined by the Legislature."
  — Cal. Const. art. XIII A, § 2(h)(1) (former provision, inoperative for transfers on or after February 16, 2021), California Constitution, the pre-Proposition 19 parent-child exclusion, quoted for contrast (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.+2.&article=XIII+A)
  Known gap: Two independent sources state today's rule — Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(1) (statute) and Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(5) (constitution) — and a third, separately enacted and now-superseded constitutional provision, Article XIII A, Section 2(h)(1), is cited only to state precisely what the pre-February-16-2021 rule required, for contrast; it does not describe current law. This clause addresses the family-home version of the requirement; Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(d) extends the identical mechanism to a family farm, addressed in this document's clause on the family farm and non-residence-property rules. This clause does not determine whether any specific property has become, or will become, any specific transferee's principal residence, or whether any specific transferee has timely filed for either exemption.

THE CURRENT TAXABLE-VALUE FORMULA FOR AN EXCLUDED FAMILY HOME OR FAMILY FARM
Rather than excluding a family home or family farm from reassessment outright, the current rule caps how much of any increase in value is added to the transferred property's taxable value. Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(d) states that the new taxable value of an excluded family home or family farm is the sum of (1) the taxable value the property already carried immediately before the transfer, and (2) an additional amount that depends on a comparison: if the property's fair market value upon transfer is less than that existing taxable value plus $1,000,000, the additional amount is zero; if that fair market value is equal to or more than the existing taxable value plus $1,000,000, the additional amount equals the fair market value minus the sum of the existing taxable value and $1,000,000. In effect, only the amount by which fair market value exceeds the prior taxable value plus $1,000,000 is added to the property's new taxable value; the transferred property does not receive a full reassessment to current fair market value. Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(1)(B) of the California Constitution states the same two-branch formula for a family home, describing the comparison value as the property's "assessed value" rather than, as the statute does, its "fair market value."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The new taxable value of the family home or family farm shall be the sum of both of the following:(1) The taxable value of the family home or family farm as determined in accordance with Section 110.1, with the adjustments permitted by subdivision (b) of Section 2 of Article XIII A of the California Constitution and subdivision (f) of Section 110.1, determined as of the date immediately prior to the date the principal residence or family farm is purchased or transferred to the transferee.(2) The applicable of the following amounts:(A) If the fair market value, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 110, of the family home or family farm upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee is less than the sum of the taxable value described in paragraph (1) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), then zero dollars ($0).(B) If the fair market value, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 110, of the family home or family farm upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee is equal to or more than the sum of the taxable value described in paragraph (1) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), an amount equal to the fair market value of the family home upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee, minus the sum of the taxable value described in paragraph (1) and one million dollars ($1,000,000)."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 63.2(d), California Revenue and Taxation Code, new taxable value formula for an excluded family home or family farm (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=63.2.)
  "(B) The applicable of the following amounts:(i) If the assessed value of the family home upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee is less than the sum of the taxable value described in subparagraph (A) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), then zero dollars ($0).(ii) If the assessed value of the family home upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee is equal to or more than the sum of the taxable value described in subparagraph (A) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), an amount equal to the assessed value of the family home upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee, minus the sum of the taxable value described in subparagraph (A) and one million dollars ($1,000,000)."
  — Cal. Const. art. XIII A, § 2.1(c)(1)(B), California Constitution, parallel taxable-value formula for a family home (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.+2.1.&article=XIII+A)
  Known gap: Two independently enacted sources state this formula in materially the same terms — Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(d) (statute) and Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(1) (constitution) — and are treated here as independent. This clause notes, without resolving it, a terminology difference between the two texts: the statute frames the comparison using the property's "fair market value... as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 110," while the constitutional provision uses "assessed value" for the same comparison; this document does not determine whether that difference in wording produces any difference in outcome. This clause states the formula in general terms; it does not compute the resulting taxable value for the property described in this document, which depends on that property's own prior taxable value and its fair market value on the date of transfer.

BIENNIAL INFLATION ADJUSTMENT OF THE $1,000,000 FIGURE
The $1,000,000 figure used in the current taxable-value formula is not fixed permanently at that dollar amount. Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(4) of the California Constitution states that, beginning on February 16, 2023, and every other February 16 after that, the State Board of Equalization must adjust the $1,000,000 amount for inflation, to reflect the percentage change in the House Price Index for California for the preceding calendar year, as determined by the Federal Housing Finance Agency, and that the State Board of Equalization calculates and publishes the resulting adjustment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Beginning on February 16, 2023, and every other February 16 thereafter, the State Board of Equalization shall adjust the one million dollar ($1,000,000) amount described in paragraph (1) for inflation to reflect the percentage change in the House Price Index for California for the prior calendar year, as determined by the Federal Housing Finance Agency."
  — Cal. Const. art. XIII A, § 2.1(c)(4), California Constitution, biennial inflation adjustment of the $1,000,000 exclusion amount (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.+2.1.&article=XIII+A)
  Known gap: This inflation-adjustment mechanism is stated only in Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(4) of the California Constitution; the implementing statute, Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(d), states the taxable-value formula using a flat "one million dollars ($1,000,000)" figure and does not itself repeat or cross-reference the adjustment mechanism in its own text. This clause is therefore based on a single verified source, not independently corroborated by the statute's own wording, and that gap between the statute's flat figure and the constitution's adjustment instruction is stated here as a fact about the text of each provision, not resolved as a claim about which figure a county assessor applies to any particular transfer in any given year. This clause does not state the currently adjusted dollar figure for any specific year, which was not independently verified in this research.

FAMILY FARMS AND THE END OF THE GENERAL EXCLUSION FOR NON-RESIDENCE PROPERTY
The current exclusion reaches only two categories of property: a family home that meets the principal-residence conditions described elsewhere in this document, and a family farm. Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(2) extends the same exclusion mechanism to "a family farm of an eligible transferor," applying it separately to each legal parcel making up the farm, except that a parcel containing a family home is instead evaluated under the family-home rule. This differs from the exclusion that applied to transfers before February 16, 2021, which — as described in this document's clause on the pre-2021 rule — also excluded up to $1,000,000 of full cash value of "other real property" between parents and children generally, with no requirement that the property be a farm or that the transferee use it as a residence. The current statute contains no comparable general exclusion for other real property that is neither a principal residence nor a family farm. Article XIII A, Section 2.1(a)(2) of the California Constitution states the Legislature's and voters' stated purpose in adopting this narrower scope: to protect the ability of parents and grandparents to pass on a family home for continued use as a primary residence, while ending the exclusion as applied to vacation homes, income properties, and other non-residence real property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The purchase or transfer is of a family farm of an eligible transferor in the case of a purchase or transfer between parents and their children or between grandparents and their grandchildren, if all of the parents, other than stepparents, of that grandchild or those grandchildren, who qualify as the children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of purchase or transfer."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 63.2(a)(2), California Revenue and Taxation Code, family farm exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=63.2.)
  "Limit property tax increases on family homes used as a primary residence by protecting the right of parents and grandparents to pass on their family home to their children and grandchildren for continued use as a primary residence, while eliminating unfair tax loopholes used by East Coast investors, celebrities, wealthy non-California residents, and trust fund heirs to avoid paying a fair share of property taxes on vacation homes, income properties, and beachfront rentals they own in California."
  — Cal. Const. art. XIII A, § 2.1(a)(2), California Constitution, stated purpose narrowing the exclusion to residence and farm property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.+2.1.&article=XIII+A)
  Known gap: This states two independent sources: Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(2) (the statutory family-farm provision) and Article XIII A, Section 2.1(a)(2) (a constitutional statement of purpose accompanying the same measure). The statement-of-purpose language is cited to confirm the general direction of the change — narrowing the exclusion to residence and farm property — not as an operative rule with independent legal force apart from the operative text of Section 63.2(a) itself, which by its own structure lists only a principal residence (paragraph (1)) and a family farm (paragraph (2)) as excluded categories. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific parcel is, in fact, a family farm within the statutory definition, which depends on the property's actual use.

THE GRANDPARENT-GRANDCHILD TRANSFER'S OWN ELIGIBILITY CONDITION
A transfer between a grandparent and a grandchild qualifies for the same exclusion as a parent-child transfer only if an additional condition is met. Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(1) extends the family-home exclusion to a transfer "between grandparents and their grandchildren" only "if all of the parents, other than stepparents, of that grandchild or those grandchildren, who qualify as the children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of purchase or transfer," and the same statute applies an identical condition to the family-farm exclusion in § 63.2(a)(2). Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(2) of the California Constitution states the same condition for a family-home transfer between grandparents and grandchildren: it applies "if all of the parents of those grandchildren, who qualify as children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of the purchase or transfer." In substance, the grandparent-grandchild exclusion is unavailable while a grandchild's parent — a child of the grandparent — is still living, unless that living parent is only a stepparent to the grandchild.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The purchase or transfer of real property that is the principal residence of an eligible transferor in the case of a purchase or transfer between parents and their children or between grandparents and their grandchildren, if all of the parents, other than stepparents, of that grandchild or those grandchildren, who qualify as the children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of purchase or transfer."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 63.2(a)(1), California Revenue and Taxation Code, deceased-parents condition for a grandparent-grandchild transfer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=63.2.)
  "Paragraph (1) shall also apply to a purchase or transfer of the family home between grandparents and their grandchildren if all of the parents of those grandchildren, who qualify as children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of the purchase or transfer."
  — Cal. Const. art. XIII A, § 2.1(c)(2), California Constitution, parallel deceased-parents condition for a grandparent-grandchild transfer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.+2.1.&article=XIII+A)
  Known gap: This states two independent sources: Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(1) (statute) and Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(2) (constitution). A precise nuance worth flagging: the statutory text expressly carves out stepparents ("other than stepparents") from the deceased-parent condition, while the constitutional text quoted here states the condition without that express stepparent carve-out appearing in this particular passage. This clause does not resolve that wording difference or determine how it would apply to any specific grandchild's family circumstances; it states what each text says. This clause addresses only the deceased-parents eligibility condition; it does not restate the principal-residence and homeowners'/disabled-veterans'-exemption requirements described elsewhere in this document, which apply to a qualifying grandparent-grandchild transfer in the same way they apply to a parent-child transfer.

SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION
Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee certify that the information stated in this information sheet is true and correct to the best of their knowledge. Executed on September 2, 2026, at Sacramento, California.

Transferor: Pat Morgan _________________________ Date: September 2, 2026

Transferee: Jordan Lee _________________________ Date: September 2, 2026

This certification confirms only that the information above was reviewed and signed. It is not the claim for exclusion described in Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(b), which must be filed separately with the county assessor for the property described in this document, and it is not a determination by any assessor, the State Board of Equalization, or any other authority that this transfer qualifies for exclusion from reassessment.

Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(d) states that the new taxable value of an excluded family home or family farm is the sum of (1) the taxable value the property already carried immediately before the transfer, and (2) an additional amount that depends on a comparison: if the property's fair market value upon transfer is less than that existing taxable value plus $1,000,000, the additional amount is zero; if that fair market value is equal to or more than the existing taxable value plus $1,000,000, the additional amount equals the fair market value minus the sum of the existing taxable value and $1,000,000. In effect, only the amount by which fair market value exceeds the prior taxable value plus $1,000,000 is added to the property's new taxable value; the transferred property does not receive a full reassessment to current fair market value. Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(1)(B) of the California Constitution states the same two-branch formula for a family home, describing the comparison value as the property's "assessed value" rather than, as the statute does, its "fair market value."

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, new taxable value formula for an excluded family home or family farm
citations.quote: The new taxable value of the family home or family farm shall be the sum of both of the following:(1) The taxable value of the family home or family farm as determined in accordance with Section 110.1, with the adjustments permitted by subdivision (b) of Section 2 of Article XIII A of the California Constitution and subdivision (f) of Section 110.1, determined as of the date immediately prior to the date the principal residence or family farm is purchased or transferred to the transferee.(2) The applicable of the following amounts:(A) If the fair market value, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 110, of the family home or family farm upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee is less than the sum of the taxable value described in paragraph (1) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), then zero dollars ($0).(B) If the fair market value, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 110, of the family home or family farm upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee is equal to or more than the sum of the taxable value described in paragraph (1) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), an amount equal to the fair market value of the family home upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee, minus the sum of the taxable value described in paragraph (1) and one million dollars ($1,000,000).

citations.cite: California Constitution, parallel taxable-value formula for a family home
citations.quote: (B) The applicable of the following amounts:(i) If the assessed value of the family home upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee is less than the sum of the taxable value described in subparagraph (A) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), then zero dollars ($0).(ii) If the assessed value of the family home upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee is equal to or more than the sum of the taxable value described in subparagraph (A) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), an amount equal to the assessed value of the family home upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee, minus the sum of the taxable value described in subparagraph (A) and one million dollars ($1,000,000).

expectedJSON.gap: Two independently enacted sources state this formula in materially the same terms — Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(d) (statute) and Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(1) (constitution) — and are treated here as independent. This clause notes, without resolving it, a terminology difference between the two texts: the statute frames the comparison using the property's "fair market value... as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 110," while the constitutional provision uses "assessed value" for the same comparison; this document does not determine whether that difference in wording produces any difference in outcome. This clause states the formula in general terms; it does not compute the resulting taxable value for the property described in this document, which depends on that property's own prior taxable value and its fair market value on the date of transfer.

expectedJSON.body: The $1,000,000 figure used in the current taxable-value formula is not fixed permanently at that dollar amount. Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(4) of the California Constitution states that, beginning on February 16, 2023, and every other February 16 after that, the State Board of Equalization must adjust the $1,000,000 amount for inflation, to reflect the percentage change in the House Price Index for California for the preceding calendar year, as determined by the Federal Housing Finance Agency, and that the State Board of Equalization calculates and publishes the resulting adjustment.

citations.cite: California Constitution, biennial inflation adjustment of the $1,000,000 exclusion amount
citations.quote: Beginning on February 16, 2023, and every other February 16 thereafter, the State Board of Equalization shall adjust the one million dollar ($1,000,000) amount described in paragraph (1) for inflation to reflect the percentage change in the House Price Index for California for the prior calendar year, as determined by the Federal Housing Finance Agency.

expectedJSON.gap: This inflation-adjustment mechanism is stated only in Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(4) of the California Constitution; the implementing statute, Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(d), states the taxable-value formula using a flat "one million dollars ($1,000,000)" figure and does not itself repeat or cross-reference the adjustment mechanism in its own text. This clause is therefore based on a single verified source, not independently corroborated by the statute's own wording, and that gap between the statute's flat figure and the constitution's adjustment instruction is stated here as a fact about the text of each provision, not resolved as a claim about which figure a county assessor applies to any particular transfer in any given year. This clause does not state the currently adjusted dollar figure for any specific year, which was not independently verified in this research.

expectedJSON.body: The current exclusion reaches only two categories of property: a family home that meets the principal-residence conditions described elsewhere in this document, and a family farm. Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(2) extends the same exclusion mechanism to "a family farm of an eligible transferor," applying it separately to each legal parcel making up the farm, except that a parcel containing a family home is instead evaluated under the family-home rule. This differs from the exclusion that applied to transfers before February 16, 2021, which — as described in this document's clause on the pre-2021 rule — also excluded up to $1,000,000 of full cash value of "other real property" between parents and children generally, with no requirement that the property be a farm or that the transferee use it as a residence. The current statute contains no comparable general exclusion for other real property that is neither a principal residence nor a family farm. Article XIII A, Section 2.1(a)(2) of the California Constitution states the Legislature's and voters' stated purpose in adopting this narrower scope: to protect the ability of parents and grandparents to pass on a family home for continued use as a primary residence, while ending the exclusion as applied to vacation homes, income properties, and other non-residence real property.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, family farm exclusion
citations.quote: The purchase or transfer is of a family farm of an eligible transferor in the case of a purchase or transfer between parents and their children or between grandparents and their grandchildren, if all of the parents, other than stepparents, of that grandchild or those grandchildren, who qualify as the children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of purchase or transfer.

citations.cite: California Constitution, stated purpose narrowing the exclusion to residence and farm property
citations.quote: Limit property tax increases on family homes used as a primary residence by protecting the right of parents and grandparents to pass on their family home to their children and grandchildren for continued use as a primary residence, while eliminating unfair tax loopholes used by East Coast investors, celebrities, wealthy non-California residents, and trust fund heirs to avoid paying a fair share of property taxes on vacation homes, income properties, and beachfront rentals they own in California.

expectedJSON.gap: This states two independent sources: Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(2) (the statutory family-farm provision) and Article XIII A, Section 2.1(a)(2) (a constitutional statement of purpose accompanying the same measure). The statement-of-purpose language is cited to confirm the general direction of the change — narrowing the exclusion to residence and farm property — not as an operative rule with independent legal force apart from the operative text of Section 63.2(a) itself, which by its own structure lists only a principal residence (paragraph (1)) and a family farm (paragraph (2)) as excluded categories. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific parcel is, in fact, a family farm within the statutory definition, which depends on the property's actual use.

expectedJSON.body: A transfer between a grandparent and a grandchild qualifies for the same exclusion as a parent-child transfer only if an additional condition is met. Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(1) extends the family-home exclusion to a transfer "between grandparents and their grandchildren" only "if all of the parents, other than stepparents, of that grandchild or those grandchildren, who qualify as the children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of purchase or transfer," and the same statute applies an identical condition to the family-farm exclusion in § 63.2(a)(2). Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(2) of the California Constitution states the same condition for a family-home transfer between grandparents and grandchildren: it applies "if all of the parents of those grandchildren, who qualify as children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of the purchase or transfer." In substance, the grandparent-grandchild exclusion is unavailable while a grandchild's parent — a child of the grandparent — is still living, unless that living parent is only a stepparent to the grandchild.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, deceased-parents condition for a grandparent-grandchild transfer
citations.quote: The purchase or transfer of real property that is the principal residence of an eligible transferor in the case of a purchase or transfer between parents and their children or between grandparents and their grandchildren, if all of the parents, other than stepparents, of that grandchild or those grandchildren, who qualify as the children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of purchase or transfer.

citations.cite: California Constitution, parallel deceased-parents condition for a grandparent-grandchild transfer
citations.quote: Paragraph (1) shall also apply to a purchase or transfer of the family home between grandparents and their grandchildren if all of the parents of those grandchildren, who qualify as children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of the purchase or transfer.

expectedJSON.gap: This states two independent sources: Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(1) (statute) and Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(2) (constitution). A precise nuance worth flagging: the statutory text expressly carves out stepparents ("other than stepparents") from the deceased-parent condition, while the constitutional text quoted here states the condition without that express stepparent carve-out appearing in this particular passage. This clause does not resolve that wording difference or determine how it would apply to any specific grandchild's family circumstances; it states what each text says. This clause addresses only the deceased-parents eligibility condition; it does not restate the principal-residence and homeowners'/disabled-veterans'-exemption requirements described elsewhere in this document, which apply to a qualifying grandparent-grandchild transfer in the same way they apply to a parent-child transfer.
